skip_reason: Inbound scheduling and logistics call on a job that was already quoted and sold, not a new-business sales conversation. Mary Kay calls in pre-sold - 'Okay, hey, I'd like to go ahead and schedule you guys for a move' - and Calvin pulls up an existing record ('let me pull up your profile so we can get that sorted') from a prior quote he had already emailed her, which he references directly ('I should have linked it in the email... cause I put the oasis cleaning and it was like right before that'). The entire call is date confirmation for the Oct 12 pack and Oct 13 move, advice on where to site a storage unit and what size and door to get, and a Sparefoot referral. There is no intake, no quote form recap, no hourly rate, no clock explanation, no estimate, no differentiator pitch and no booking attempt - the selling happened on an earlier call. Applying the 85-point sales scorecard here would auto-grant the pricing, clock, estimate and Save Your Ass sections under the N/A rule and produce a score that measures nothing about this rep's selling.
top_strength: Calvin's referral habit paid off in front of him on this call, which is the kind of proof worth showing the rest of the team. He had put a cleaning company in an earlier email and she acted on it - 'I did contact oasis and I am gonna hire them to come in. So thanks for that lead, yeah, so I appreciate that' - and he did it again live when she got stuck on the storage unit: 'I don't know if you browse that spare foot.com at all, but it's a pretty good resource,' followed by the practical steer that 'a lot of storage unit places. It's like, you know, first month free or that sort of thing.' He also gave her genuinely customer-first advice against his own convenience. She repeatedly tried to optimize the storage location for the crew - 'Saves, saves you driving to dripping springs and such' and 'you tell me what would be better for you guys' - and instead of steering her, he handed the decision back: 'whatever is going to be more convenient for you. As far as like, where the storage unit will be, will be fine.' The one operational detail he did volunteer was the one that actually matters to the bill - 'ideally there's not like an elevator involved that's just gonna just a time' - and he closed by confirming the concrete logistics without being asked: the Oct 12 pack, the Oct 13 move, 'an 8:30 AM to 9:00 AM arrival time on each day,' and a clear instruction to email the storage address once she has it. She ended on 'Thanks Calvin. I appreciate you.'
coaching_note: Not scored against the sales rubric - this is post-sale scheduling on a job Calvin already quoted, and it should be routed out of the sales grading average. Two things are still worth naming. First, there is a second move sitting on this call that nobody put on a calendar. The load-out of storage is real revenue, Mary Kay volunteered the timing driver herself ('My painting guy says he needs 1010 to fourteen days'), and Calvin handed it back to her twice - 'once you know that you can just give me a call and I can get you scheduled for the move out of storage.' A customer who has not yet rented the unit and is waiting on a painter is a customer who will forget to call. The better move is to own the follow-up: 'Let me set a reminder to check in with you the week of the twenty-seventh - if your painter's timeline is firm by then we'll book the load-out, and if not I'll try you again the week after.' Second, the email he promised is a plain confirmation, not the handoff the scorecard wants. He said 'I'll send over the confirmation email for the packing on the twelfth the moving on the thirteenth' with no ask to verify it. On a job with two dates, a storage stop with no address yet, and a second move still unscheduled, 'look it over and reply if anything's off, especially the dates' costs three seconds and is the cheapest protection against a wrong-day crew dispatch there is.
phone_presence_notes: Relaxed, unhurried and genuinely helpful - he let her think out loud through the storage decision without rushing her, gave a referral that had already earned her trust once ('Cool, yeah, definitely glad that worked out'), and she closed with 'Thanks Calvin. I appreciate you,' which is rapport she volunteered rather than politeness he asked for.
